title: 6 GHz Spectrum & 320 MHz Channels
summary: A wide, uncrowded band and channels twice as wide as Wi-Fi 6E allows.

opener.promise: A wide, clean new band with much wider channels
opener.problem: Crowded older bands cap capacity, however many access points you add.

wifi7Adds: Wi-Fi 7 adds 320 MHz channels in the 6 GHz band, twice the widest channel Wi-Fi 6E can use {{eht-max-width}} {{width-320-vs-160}}.

beats.heading: Too many devices, too few lanes

caption.headline: Too many devices, too few lanes
caption.takeaway: Older bands are crowded and slowed by [[legacy-device|legacy devices]]; adding access points eventually stops helping.

beats.body:
On a busy medical-surgical floor, every badge, pump, monitor and workstation shares the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands — along with older devices, guest phones and the unit next door.

Those bands only fit a handful of wide channels, and older [[legacy-device|legacy devices]] slow every channel they share, because newer devices must fall back to methods the older ones understand.
beats.bottomLine: Adding more access points in crowded bands eventually stops helping; capacity is limited by the spectrum itself.
beats.sceneDescription: Three roads leave an access point, one per band, each drawn as wide as its band. The narrow 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz roads are jammed: grey trucks for older devices crawl along and hold up the cars behind them, while the much wider 6 GHz road beside them sits unlit and empty.

callout.title: Why the old bands run out
points: The 2.4 and 5 GHz bands fit only a handful of wide channels
[[legacy-device|Older devices]] make everyone sharing their channel slow down
Guest phones and neighbouring units crowd the same channels
More access points stop helping once every channel is taken

hotspots.technical: Newer devices on the same channel must fall back to older, slower ways of sharing it.

beats.heading: A new band, and wider lanes inside it

caption.headline: A new band, wider than the rest combined
caption.takeaway: The US opened 1200 MHz{{us-6ghz-total}} for Wi-Fi; Wi-Fi 7 adds 320 MHz channels there{{eht-max-width}}.

beats.body:
Wi-Fi 6E opened the 6 GHz band to Wi-Fi {{wifi6e-6ghz-origin}}. In the United States it adds 1200 MHz of spectrum {{us-6ghz-total}}, running from 5925 to 7125 MHz {{us-6ghz-band-start}} {{us-6ghz-band-end}}.

Wi-Fi 7 adds 320 MHz channels, which are only available in the 6 GHz band {{320mhz-6ghz-only}}.
beats.bottomLine: 6 GHz is the largest block of new Wi-Fi spectrum in a generation, and Wi-Fi 7 is designed to make the most of it.
beats.sceneDescription: The 6 GHz road lights up. Drawn to the same frequency scale, it is wider than the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz roads together, and no older devices travel on it.

questions.q: Will our existing devices use the new band?
questions.a: Only devices built for Wi-Fi 6E or later can operate in 6 GHz{{6ghz-no-legacy}}. Older devices stay on 2.4 and 5 GHz{{6ghz-no-legacy}}, and still benefit because capable devices move off those bands.

callout.title: What 6 GHz adds
points: 1200 MHz of new spectrum for Wi-Fi in the US{{us-6ghz-total}}
Only Wi-Fi 6E and newer devices can use it{{6ghz-no-legacy}}: no legacy slowdowns
Room for channels too wide to fit in the older bands{{320mhz-6ghz-only}}

beats.heading: Room for more channels, and wider ones

caption.headline: Room for more channels, and wider ones
caption.takeaway: The US band fits 59 channels of 20 MHz{{us-6ghz-channels-20}} or three of 320 MHz{{us-6ghz-channels-320}}.
caption.technical: Only Wi-Fi 6E and newer devices operate there{{6ghz-no-legacy}}; [[lpi|low-power indoor]] access points may use the whole band{{fcc-lpi}}.

beats.body:
With 1200 MHz available {{us-6ghz-total}}, the US 6 GHz band fits 59 channels of 20 MHz {{us-6ghz-channels-20}}, 29 of 40 MHz {{us-6ghz-channels-40}}, 14 of 80 MHz {{us-6ghz-channels-80}}, 7 of 160 MHz {{us-6ghz-channels-160}} or 3 non-overlapping channels of 320 MHz {{us-6ghz-channels-320}}.

The band is also clean: only Wi-Fi 6E and newer devices can operate there {{6ghz-no-legacy}}, so no [[legacy-device|legacy devices]] slow it down. Low-power indoor access points can use the whole band {{fcc-lpi}}.
beats.bottomLine: More, wider, uncongested channels means more capacity per access point and fewer devices competing on each channel.
beats.deepDive: Channel counts follow from the band edges and the 6 GHz channel raster, which starts at 5945 MHz {{6ghz-ch1-lower-edge}}; each count is recomputed from those inputs. [[lpi|LPI]] access points may operate across the band without coordination {{fcc-lpi}}. [[channel-width|Channel width]] is a trade-off: wider channels carry more per transmission, but fewer fit, which matters when neighbouring [[access-point|access points]] must avoid each other. Availability differs by [[regulatory-domain]]: the European harmonised band covers 5945–6425 MHz {{eu-6ghz-band}}.
beats.sceneDescription: Lane markings divide the 6 GHz road into four stretches: many narrow 20 MHz lanes, then 80 MHz and 160 MHz lanes, and finally three wide 320 MHz lanes, each stretch labelled with how many lanes fit {{us-6ghz-channels-20}} {{us-6ghz-channels-80}} {{us-6ghz-channels-160}} {{us-6ghz-channels-320}}. Traffic flows freely in every lane.

questions.q: Why not use the widest channels everywhere?
questions.a: Only three fit in the US band{{us-6ghz-channels-320}}, so neighbouring access points would overlap. Dense floors usually run narrower channels and keep the widest ones for lightly shared areas such as imaging rooms.

callout.title: Why more channels help
points: Neighbouring access points each get their own channel and stop competing
Fewer devices share each channel, so each one waits less
Narrow channels serve many small devices; wide ones move big files fast
The US band fits three 320 MHz channels{{us-6ghz-channels-320}}

beats.heading: Twice the widest channel

caption.headline: Twice the widest channel
caption.takeaway: Large imaging files move markedly faster when each channel is twice as wide{{width-320-vs-160}}.
caption.technical: 3920 data subcarriers in 320 MHz versus 1960 in 160 MHz{{eht-nsd-320}}{{he-nsd-160}}.

beats.body:
Wi-Fi 6E's widest channel is 160 MHz {{he-max-width}}. Wi-Fi 7 doubles it to 320 MHz {{eht-max-width}} {{width-320-vs-160}}, so a single transmission can carry roughly twice as much data under the same conditions.

Wi-Fi 5 and earlier cannot use 6 GHz at all {{6ghz-no-legacy}}.
beats.bottomLine: For data-heavy areas such as imaging and procedure rooms, Wi-Fi 7 can move large files markedly faster on the same spectrum.
beats.deepDive: Doubling channel width doubles the data subcarriers per symbol (3920 in 320 MHz versus 1960 in 160 MHz) {{eht-nsd-320}} {{he-nsd-160}}. In practice, 320 MHz channels {{eht-max-width}} suit lightly shared areas; dense floors often use narrower channels so neighbouring access points can reuse spectrum, with [[preamble-puncturing|preamble puncturing]] helping wide channels survive interference (see the next chapter).
beats.sceneDescription: The 6 GHz road is split in two. On the left, the earlier generation’s seven 160 MHz lanes {{us-6ghz-channels-160}} carry mid-sized vehicles; on the right, Wi-Fi 7’s three 320 MHz lanes {{us-6ghz-channels-320}} carry trucks twice as wide. Choosing Wi-Fi 5 or Wi-Fi 6 closes the left half, because those devices cannot use 6 GHz.

callout.title: Why Wi-Fi 7 is faster here
points: Its widest channel is twice as wide as Wi-Fi 6E’s{{width-320-vs-160}}
Twice the width carries about twice the data per transmission{{eht-nsd-320}}{{he-nsd-160}}
Imaging files and video consults finish sooner, freeing [[airtime|airtime]] for others
Wi-Fi 5 and Wi-Fi 6 devices cannot use 6 GHz at all{{6ghz-no-legacy}}

hotspots.technical: A 320 MHz channel carries 3920 data subcarriers per symbol versus 1960 at 160 MHz{{eht-nsd-320}}{{he-nsd-160}}.

beats.heading: Big files and live video, in the right places

caption.headline: Big files and video, in the right places
caption.takeaway: 6 GHz fades through walls{{6ghz-building-loss}}: plan coverage with a site survey and check local rules.
caption.technical: Rules differ by [[regulatory-domain|regulatory domain]]: Europe harmonises only 5945–6425 MHz{{eu-6ghz-band}}.

beats.body:
Imaging transfers, telehealth video and remote consults benefit most from wide, clean channels. They can move to 6 GHz, leaving 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz for devices that cannot.

There is a trade-off: walls and building materials weaken 6 GHz signals {{6ghz-building-loss}}, so coverage needs planning, and rules differ between countries {{eu-6ghz-band}}.
beats.bottomLine: 6 GHz adds capacity where it is needed most, but it requires a site survey and may change access-point placement; check the rules for each country you operate in.
beats.sceneDescription: An access point inside a room sends three coverage rings through the surrounding walls: the 2.4 GHz ring reaches furthest, the 5 GHz ring less far and the 6 GHz ring is the most contained. The rings are labelled as illustrative.

questions.q: Do we need more access points for the new band?
questions.a: Possibly in some areas. Walls weaken 6 GHz signals more than lower bands{{6ghz-building-loss}}, so a site survey decides placement. Many designs reuse existing locations; run the survey before you budget.

questions.q: Does this work outside the United States?
questions.a: Rules vary by country. Europe harmonises the lower part of the band, 5945–6425 MHz{{eu-6ghz-band}}, so fewer wide channels fit. Check each country’s regulator before designing.

keyFigures.note: Fewer, wider channels: 320 MHz channels {{eht-max-width}} suit areas with few neighbouring access points.
Other regions allow less; Europe harmonises the lower part of the band.
